messages.content: Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to Payments

Run a payment end to end in sandbox during your first week, and be able to explain what happened at each hop. That's the whole goal, and everything below serves it.

Start with access. Ask your onboarding buddy for the payments-dev VPN profile, a sandbox merchant account, and read access to the ledger replica. Requests go through the platform team and usually clear in a day, so file them before you start reading. While you wait, skim the service map so the names in those documents mean something when you get to them.

Then read three documents, in this order. The ledger schema note explains why every balance change is two rows and never an update. The idempotency guide explains why every write endpoint requires a client-supplied key. The settlement timeline explains why a payment that looks finished on Monday can still fail on Wednesday.

Two rules matter more than the rest. We do not mutate or delete a ledger row; a correction is a new entry that references the old one. And we do not treat a processor callback as truth; we reconcile against the end-of-day file and let that win. Both rules have cost us money when someone forgot them.

Your first ticket is small on purpose. It is normally something in the refund path, where the code is well covered and the blast radius is low. Pair on it with whoever reviews your access requests. Nobody here ships their first payments change alone, and asking early costs the team far less than a bad reconciliation.
Add a section on who to ask for what.

Here's the section to add at the end:

## Who to ask for what

Access, VPN, and anything that needs an approval you can't grant yourself goes to your onboarding buddy first. They know which requests the platform team handles and which ones need a manager signature, and they'll save you a day of guessing.

For the ledger, ask in #payments-ledger. The people who wrote the double-entry schema read that channel, and they would rather answer a question than review a migration that got the sign wrong.

For processor behaviour, quirks in callbacks, retry semantics, anything that smells like the other side is misbehaving, ask in #payments-processors. Include the payment reference and the processor name in your first message; it's the first thing anyone will ask for.

For on-call and anything happening right now in production, page through the payments rotation rather than posting in a channel. Channels are for questions that can wait an hour. If money is moving wrong, it can't wait an hour.

For everything else, ask your manager in your weekly one-to-one, or sooner if it's blocking you. Nothing here is a test.

## Who to ask for what

Access, VPN, and anything needing an approval you can't grant yourself goes to your onboarding buddy first. They know which requests the platform team handles and which ones need a manager signature, and they'll save you a day of guessing. Nothing here is a test, so ask early.

For the ledger, ask in #payments-ledger. The people who wrote the double-entry schema read that channel. They would rather answer a question than review a migration that got the sign wrong.

For processor behaviour, ask in #payments-processors. That covers quirks in callbacks, retry semantics, and anything that smells like the other side is misbehaving. Include the payment reference and the processor name in your first message; it's the first thing anyone will ask for.

For on-call and anything happening right now in production, page through the payments rotation rather than posting in a channel. Channels are for questions that can wait an hour. If money is moving wrong, it can't wait an hour, and nobody will mind being paged over it.

For everything else, ask your manager. The weekly one-to-one is the normal place for it, but go sooner if the thing is blocking you.
